content.text:
The download bar is reworked. What changed:

**Progress that reflects reality** — `web/src/lib/model-download-progress.ts` (new, pure, unit-tested)
- transformers.js reports progress *per file*; the old code read `progress.progress` off the newest event, so the bar rewound to 0 every time a shard started. The tracker now sums bytes across every file it has seen.
- The catalog's `downloadLabel` ("~4.5 GB") is parsed and used as a denominator floor, so the bar doesn't read 90% while only `config.json` has announced its size. It's monotonic against a fixed denominator (a retried range request can't rewind it) and rescales only when a new file announces a size — better than pinning at 99% for the rest of a multi-GB download.
- Rate and ETA come from an 8s moving window measured against *now*, so a stalled transfer decays toward 0 B/s instead of reporting the pre-stall rate.

**More honest states** — `web/src/stores/local-model.ts`
- Phases: `checking` (GPU probe) → `preparing` → `downloading` → `preparing` → ready. The final `preparing` fires once every file has been done for 1.2s, which is when the wait stops being network and becomes WebGPU graph compilation — previously that was a bar frozen at 100%. Cached loads emit no progress events at all and now say "Preparing model…" instead of sitting at 0%.
- Repaints throttled to ~140ms, so a fast download no longer re-renders the selector hundreds of times a second.

**The bar itself** — `web/src/components/ModelDownloadBar.tsx` (new)
- Headline + percent, bar, and a detail line: `1.2 GB of 4.5 GB · 18 MB/s · about 3 min left`.
- Uses `var(--primary)` instead of the hardcoded `#2563eb`, so it follows the theme. Drifting stripes on the fill (a multi-GB download can look frozen for a minute at fixed width) and a sweep animation when the size is unknown; both collapse under `prefers-reduced-motion`.
- `role="progressbar"` with `aria-valuenow`/`aria-valuetext`, omitted while indeterminate so screen readers announce busy rather than a fake number.

**Console** — dropped the routine `[local-model] loading…` / `ready` logs and pinned `env.backends.onnx.logLevel = "error"`, which is where most of the load-time chatter came from. Real failures still log via `console.error`. Note transformers.js may still emit its own warnings; that's inside the library.

`bun run typecheck` clean; `bun test` 701 pass, 0 fail, including 13 new tracker tests. Two panda keyframes were added to `web/panda.config.ts`.

One thing I did **not** add: a cancel button. It'd be genuinely useful on a 5 GB download, but `from_pretrained` takes no abort signal, so the button would only hide the UI while the transfer kept running — worth doing properly if you want it.

content.text:
Both controls are in. What was added on top of the earlier bar work:

**Cancel** — `local-model.ts`
- `from_pretrained` accepts no `AbortSignal` (I checked the v4 bundle — no `signal` plumbing anywhere), but transformers.js routes every request through the documented `env.fetch` hook. The store swaps in a wrapper that attaches an `AbortController` signal for the duration of the load, so `cancel()` genuinely kills the in-flight transfer instead of just hiding the UI.
- Cancelling bumps the load epoch, so the `AbortError` that surfaces inside `from_pretrained` is ignored rather than rendered as a failure banner.
- The hook is restored with an ownership check: whichever of `cancel()` or the load's `finally` runs first restores it, and a newer load owning the hook stops either from clobbering it. Without that, cancel-then-retry chained wrappers and leaked the *already-aborted* signal into the retry, which would have made every subsequent load fail instantly.

**Delete** — `web/src/lib/model-cache.ts` (new) + store
- Scans and clears the two Cache API buckets transformers.js writes to (`transformers-cache`, `experimental_transformers-hash-cache`), matching entries by repo id. Sizes come from `content-length` headers only — never reads a multi-GB body to measure it.
- `localModel.removeDownload(id)` unloads first when it's the live model, so the delete frees GPU memory as well as disk.
- Cache names are hardcoded to the library defaults deliberately: importing `@huggingface/transformers` just to read `env.cacheKey` would pull ~100MB into the bundle for a cache scan.

**UI** — `ModelDownloadBar.tsx`, `useCachedModelSize.ts` (new hook)
- Cancel sits in the download bar's headline row; both controls `stopPropagation` so clicking them doesn't also select the model (the row is a `div onClick`, so nested buttons are valid here).
- Delete is two-step inline ("Delete download" → "Delete / Keep", or "Unload and delete?" when it's live) — a `window.confirm` would block the browser inside a modal, and these downloads are expensive to replace. Rows show `4.4 GB stored in this browser` when cached.
- One shared cache scan backs every row rather than one scan per row, invalidated by a `keating:model-cache-changed` event after a completed load, a cancel (partial files can remain), or a delete.

`bun run typecheck` clean; `bun test` 706 pass, 0 fail — 18 of those are new (tracker + cache, the latter against a fake `CacheStorage`).

Not verified in a real browser: I didn't kick off an actual multi-GB download to watch cancel/delete work end to end. The cache-layer and progress logic are covered by tests, but the `env.fetch` abort path and the Cache API deletion are only exercised against the real library at runtime — worth one manual pass with a small model (Gemma 3 270M is gone from the registry now, so the ~2.9 GB LFM 1.2B is the cheapest option) before shipping.

That error isn't a dtype config bug on our side — the model genuinely can't run in a browser.

**What's happening:** `onnx-community/gemma-4-E2B-it-qat-mobile-ONNX` publishes exactly one quantization, and I confirmed it against the HF API:

```
onnx/embed_tokens_q2f16.onnx
onnx/decoder_model_merged_q2f16.onnx
onnx/audio_encoder_q2f16.onnx
onnx/vision_encoder_fp16.onnx
```

Only `q2f16` — 2-bit. The registry entry was right that those are the only files that exist, but ONNX Runtime's `MatMulNBits` kernel hard-enforces 4-bit or 8-bit, and that's where "bits must be 4 or 8" comes from. The string appears nowhere in any JS in `node_modules` — it's inside the ORT WASM binary, so it's a compiled kernel limit, not something a dtype map can route around. There's no q4 variant to point at either: `onnx-community` publishes only two E2B repos, the plain one and this QAT one.

**What I did:**
- Removed the QAT entry, with a comment recording why and the condition for restoring it (onnxruntime-web gaining 2-bit support).
- Added a `classifyLocalModelError` branch for `bits must be` / `matmulnbits`, so any sub-4-bit export gives "ships weights quantized below 4 bits, which the browser ONNX runtime cannot execute yet" instead of the raw kernel error.

Typecheck clean, 706 tests pass.

**Worth checking before this branch merges** — the same wall likely stands in front of three other entries added on `fix-browser-model-dtypes`, and all four currently claim `dtype: "q4f16"`, which doesn't match what their repos hold:

- `prism-ml/Bonsai-27B-gguf-binary` and `-ternary` — the `repoId` points at a **GGUF** repo. transformers.js loads ONNX only; there are no `onnx/*.onnx` files to fetch, so these should 404 rather than load. The ternary one is sub-4-bit besides.
- `deepgrove/maple-preview` — described in its own blurb as a ternary variant, so same kernel limit, plus a ~20 GB download.

Both questions answered, and the registry now matches reality.

## Maple's actual size

The `~20 GB` label was wrong in both directions, and size isn't the real problem:

| What | Size | Format |
|---|---|---|
| `deepgrove/maple-preview` | **40.45 GB** (9 shards) | bf16 safetensors, no ONNX |
| `ProCreations/maple-preview-webgpu-v2` | **5.31 GB** | custom `.mwg`, 2-bit |
| `deepgrove/maple-preview-GGUF` / `-2bit-mlx` | — | GGUF / MLX |

The source repo is 40 GB because the ternary weights are stored *unpacked* in bf16 — it's a `MapleForCausalLM` `trust_remote_code` model with no `onnx/` directory, so transformers.js would 404 on it immediately. Your instinct that it should be lower is right about the packed form: ~5.3 GB is what 2-bit packing actually costs. But that build (24 × 207 MB layer files plus a `manifest.json`) is a hand-rolled WebGPU runtime, not ONNX, so we can't load it either. And converting it wouldn't help — ternary hits the same `bits must be 4 or 8` kernel wall; a 4-bit re-export of 20B params would land around 10 GB, *bigger* than the 2-bit port. I removed it.

## Bonsai GGUF → ONNX: already done, just not at 27B

onnx-community has published the conversions:

| Repo | 4-bit variant | Download |
|---|---|---|
| `onnx-community/Bonsai-8B-ONNX` | q4f16 | **4.76 GB** |
| `onnx-community/Bonsai-4B-ONNX` | q4f16 | **2.34 GB** |
| `onnx-community/Bonsai-1.7B-ONNX` | q4 (no f16 export) | **1.13 GB** |

These are `Qwen3ForCausalLM` — fully supported — and each declares its external-data chunk counts in `transformers.js_config.use_external_data_format` (8B q4f16 is 3 chunks), so multi-part weights resolve without extra options. I swapped all three in; sizes are summed from the HF blob API, not estimated, so the progress bar's denominator floor is accurate.

Two dead ends worth knowing:
- **`Ternary-Bonsai-{1.7B,4B,8B}-ONNX` exist but publish q2/q2f16 only** — converted, and still unloadable for the same reason as the QAT model. Ternary is precisely what ORT can't execute.
- **No 27B ONNX exists anywhere.** The 27B ecosystem is GGUF, MLX, AWQ, and a pile of community finetunes — nobody has exported it. Converting it yourself would mean a 4-bit re-quantization (~14 GB) since the ternary form can't run, which isn't a browser download.

I also removed the `repoId` field — it was declared on the spec but never read by the load path, so it silently did nothing, and only those two GGUF entries used it.

The absent models are recorded in a comment block in `BROWSER_MODELS` with the specific reason and the condition for revisiting, so this doesn't get re-litigated later. Typecheck clean, 706 tests pass.

One consequence to flag: `Bonsai 1.7B` uses `q4`, so `needsShaderF16` returns false for it — it's now the only entry that will load on a GPU without shader-f16, which is useful given every other model in the list requires it.

**Gemma 12B: nothing browser-ready exists.** Two ONNX conversions are on the Hub, and neither works with our stack:

| Repo | Layout | Usable size | Problem |
|---|---|---|---|
| `justinchuby/gemma-4-12b-onnx` | `{precision}/{device}/{component}/model.onnx` | Q4_K_M: 7.3 GB decoder + 2.0 GB embedding ≈ **9.3 GB** | onnxruntime-genai layout, no `config.json`/`transformers.js_config`, Q4_K_M K-quants; 0 downloads |
| `Prince-1/Gemma-3-12b-pt-Onnx` | single graph + `genai_config.json` | **25.7 GB** | GenAI layout again, unquantized, and it's the *base* model, not instruction-tuned |

Both target onnxruntime-genai (the native/server runtime), which uses a different file convention than transformers.js — it wants `onnx/model_q4f16.onnx` for text models, or the four-way `embed_tokens` / `decoder_model_merged` / `vision_encoder` / `audio_encoder` split for multimodal Gemma, plus `transformers.js_config` declaring external-data chunks. `onnx-community` tops out at Gemma 4 E4B; nobody has done a 12B in that shape.

**Can I make the ONNX versions?** Not on this machine, and I'd rather tell you that than burn hours proving it:

- **No GPU** (no NVIDIA adapter), 31 GB RAM with ~21 GB free, 323 GB disk, 16 cores.
- **The toolchain isn't installed** — no torch, transformers, onnx, onnxruntime, or onnxslim.
- A 12B export means pulling ~24 GB of bf16 weights, materializing the graph with roughly 2× the model size resident, then a separate quantization pass over a ~24 GB intermediate. That OOMs on 21 GB of RAM, and CPU-only export of a 12B would run for many hours even if it fit.

What *is* feasible here: text models up to ~2B, taking hours on CPU. Anything larger needs a GPU box or Colab/Modal.

There's also a ceiling worth weighing before spending GPU time on 12B specifically. At q4f16 it lands around 7–9 GB of download and needs ~8 GB of VRAM to build the session — versus Gemma 4 E4B at 5.2 GB, which is already the heaviest entry in the list and already warns it needs a discrete GPU. The jump buys real quality, but it prices out most of the browsers that would hit it.

If you want to pursue it, the useful thing I can do from here is write the conversion pipeline — `optimum-cli export onnx` plus the transformers.js quantization script, emitting the exact repo layout the loader expects, with the `transformers.js_config` chunk counts filled in — as a script you run on a GPU machine. # Browser models

What ships in the model selector, what is queued behind it, and what has already
been ruled out. Every size below was measured from the Hugging Face blob API
(sum of the chosen dtype's `.onnx` plus its `.onnx_data*` chunks, plus tokenizer
and config files) — not read off a model card.

The registry lives in `web/src/stores/local-model.ts`. Read this file before
adding to it: most of the obvious candidates are already here with a reason.

## What a model needs to run here

Four things have to be true. Each has cost us a model.

1. **An ONNX export in the transformers.js layout.** `onnx/model_q4f16.onnx`
   for text models, or the four-way `embed_tokens` / `decoder_model_merged` /
   `vision_encoder` / `audio_encoder` split for multimodal Gemma. GGUF, MLX,
   safetensors, and onnxruntime-genai layouts are all unloadable — the loader
   fetches paths that do not exist and fails as a 404.
2. **Weights quantized to 4-bit or 8-bit.** ONNX Runtime's `MatMulNBits` kernel
   accepts nothing else; sub-4-bit weights fail at session creation with
   `bits must be 4 or 8`. That string lives in the ORT WASM binary, so no
   loader-side dtype config works around it. Ternary and q2 exports are out
   until onnxruntime-web adds support.
3. **An architecture transformers.js implements.** `lfm2`, `lfm2_moe`,
   `lfm2_vl`, `qwen3`, and the Gemma families are in; a `trust_remote_code`
   architecture with custom modeling files is not.
4. **A download and a VRAM footprint a browser can carry.** Roughly: the
   download is also what has to fit on the GPU.

Multi-part external data (`model_q4f16.onnx_data_1`, `_2`, …) is fine as long as
the repo declares chunk counts in `transformers.js_config.use_external_data_format`.
Both shipped exports do.

## Shipping

| Model | Repo | dtype | Download |
|---|---|---|---|
| LFM 2.5 2.6B | `LiquidAI/LFM2.5-2.6B-ONNX` | q4f16 | 1.55 GB |
| Gemma 4 E4B | `onnx-community/gemma-4-E4B-it-ONNX` | q4f16 | ~5.2 GB |
| Gemma 4 E2B | `onnx-community/gemma-4-E2B-it-ONNX` | q4f16 | ~3.4 GB |

LFM 2.5 2.6B is the best quality per byte available: LiquidAI's own export, and
the only LFM2.5 published as ONNX. The Gemma pair carry the multimodal path.

## Queued — verified loadable, not shipped

These meet all four requirements and were checked against the Hub. Adding one is
a registry entry and nothing more.

| Model | Repo | dtype | Download | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| LFM2 1.2B | `onnx-community/LFM2-1.2B-ONNX` | q4f16 | 0.76 GB | Previous LFM generation. Smallest option found anywhere. |
| Bonsai 8B | `onnx-community/Bonsai-8B-ONNX` | q4f16 | 4.76 GB | `Qwen3ForCausalLM`. Wants a discrete GPU. |
| Bonsai 4B | `onnx-community/Bonsai-4B-ONNX` | q4f16 | 2.34 GB | Half the download of 8B. |
| Bonsai 1.7B | `onnx-community/Bonsai-1.7B-ONNX` | q4 | 1.13 GB | No f16 4-bit export in the repo. q4 is the one entry that would run on a GPU **without** `shader-f16`. |

## Ruled out

### Sub-4-bit — blocked by the ORT kernel

Revisit only if onnxruntime-web gains 2-bit support.

- `onnx-community/gemma-4-E2B-it-qat-mobile-ONNX` — publishes only q2f16 for
  `embed_tokens`, `decoder_model_merged`, and `audio_encoder` (`vision_encoder`
  is fp16). Shipped briefly and failed in production with `bits must be 4 or 8`.
- `onnx-community/Ternary-Bonsai-{1.7B,4B,8B}-ONNX` — q2/q2f16 only. The
  conversions exist; ternary is exactly what the kernel refuses.

### No usable export

- **Maple Preview** — `deepgrove/maple-preview` is 40.45 GB of bf16 safetensors
  across 9 shards, custom `MapleForCausalLM` with `trust_remote_code`, and no
  ONNX at all. Its ternary weights are stored unpacked, which is why 20B
  parameters occupy 40 GB. The only browser build is
  `ProCreations/maple-preview-webgpu(-v2)`: 5.31 GB in a custom `.mwg` format
  with a hand-rolled WebGPU runtime — not ONNX, not loadable here. A 4-bit ONNX
  re-export would land near 10 GB, *larger* than the 2-bit port it replaced.
- **Bonsai 27B** — GGUF, MLX, and AWQ only; no ONNX export exists from anyone.
  Converting the ternary weights would still require re-quantizing to q4
  (~14 GB) to clear the kernel limit, which is past what a browser should pull.
- **Gemma 12B** — two ONNX conversions exist, both in the onnxruntime-genai
  layout (`{precision}/{device}/{component}/model.onnx`), neither with a
  `transformers.js_config`:
  - `justinchuby/gemma-4-12b-onnx` — Q4_K_M at 7.3 GB decoder + 2.0 GB
    embedding ≈ 9.3 GB.
  - `Prince-1/Gemma-3-12b-pt-Onnx` — a single 25.7 GB graph, unquantized, and
    the base model rather than the instruction-tuned one.

  Even a correct 12B export would be ~7–9 GB of download needing ~8 GB of VRAM,
  against Gemma 4 E4B at 5.2 GB, which is already the heaviest thing we ship.

## Converting a model ourselves

Nobody is going to publish the exports we want, so this is on the table — but
not on a developer laptop. A 12B export means pulling ~24 GB of bf16 weights,
materializing the graph with roughly twice the model size resident, then a
separate quantization pass over a ~24 GB intermediate. That needs a GPU box or a
hosted runner; CPU-only with ~21 GB of RAM will thrash or OOM. Text models up to
about 2B are plausible locally, in hours.

The pipeline is `optimum-cli export onnx` followed by the transformers.js
quantization script, emitting the `onnx/model_q4f16.onnx` layout and a
`transformers.js_config` with correct chunk counts. Publishing is a separate
step and belongs to whoever owns the Hugging Face account — it pushes under
their name and needs their token via `huggingface-cli login`.
